title: Greenhouse climate-control trial cuts water use by 30%
excerpt: Six months of closed-loop irrigation in our smart greenhouse shows major savings without sacrificing yield — and the controller fits on a $40 board.
body:
Six months ago we asked a simple question: how much water does a greenhouse actually need if irrigation only runs when the plants ask for it?

The answer, it turns out, is about **30% less** than a conventional timer-based schedule — with no measurable yield penalty.

## How the trial worked

We retrofitted one of our research greenhouses with a closed-loop control system:

- Capacitive soil-moisture probes in every growing bed
- Temperature and humidity sensors at canopy height
- A single low-cost controller board (under $40) running the scheduling logic
- Solenoid valves on each irrigation line

Instead of watering on a fixed timer, the controller waits until the substrate moisture drops below a crop-specific threshold, then irrigates just long enough to return to field capacity.

## What we measured

Over 26 weeks we compared the closed-loop house against an identical timer-controlled house planted with the same tomato cultivar.

> The biggest surprise wasn't the water savings — it was how much more stable the substrate moisture stayed through heat waves.

Water use dropped 30%, fertigation runoff fell by almost half, and fruit yield stayed within 2% of the control house.

## What's next

We are packaging the controller design and scheduling firmware as open hardware, and preparing on-farm trials with two partner greenhouse growers. If you operate a greenhouse and want to take part, [contact us](/contact-us).
